topics.title: The basics
topics.html:
What a model actually does

A machine learning model is a function that learns a pattern from examples instead of being hand-coded. You give it many rows of data. Each row has features (the inputs, like a user's age, phone model and the time of day) and, usually, a label (the answer you want, like "clicked the ad: yes/no"). Training means adjusting the model's internal numbers, its parameters or weights, until its guesses match the labels well.

Supervised
The data has labels and the model learns to predict them. Predicting a category (spam / not spam) is classification. Predicting a number (house price) is regression.
Unsupervised
No labels. The model finds structure on its own, such as groups of similar users (clustering) or a smaller summary of many columns (dimensionality reduction).
Reinforcement
An agent learns by trial and error, collecting rewards. Rarely needed for classic ML questions.
Hyperparameter
A setting you choose before training, such as the number of trees or the learning rate. Parameters are learned; hyperparameters are picked.

You never judge a model on the data it trained on, because it may have simply memorised it. So the data is split: a training set to learn from, a validation set to tune hyperparameters, and a test set kept aside until the very end to measure the final score honestly.

Overfitting, underfitting and the bias–variance trade-off

Imagine a student preparing for an exam.

Underfitting
The student barely studied and does badly on practice papers and the real exam. The model is too simple to capture the pattern. This is called high bias.
Overfitting
The student memorised the practice papers word for word. Perfect on those, poor on new questions. The model learned the noise in the training data. This is called high variance, because the model would change a lot if trained on a slightly different sample.

How to tell them apart

Training error high, test error high → underfitting. Fix: a more complex model, more features, less regularisation.
Training error low, test error much higher → overfitting. Fix: more data, a simpler model, regularisation, dropout, early stopping.

Making a model more flexible lowers bias but raises variance, and vice versa. The goal is the sweet spot in between. Total error = bias² + variance + noise that no model can remove.

Handy facts: a deeper decision tree → more variance. A bigger k in k-nearest-neighbours → more bias. Stronger regularisation → more bias, less variance.

Regularisation: stopping a model from overfitting

A model that overfits usually has some very large weights, leaning hard on a few features. Regularisation adds a penalty for large weights to the training loss, so the model prefers simpler explanations. The strength of the penalty is a hyperparameter, written λ (lambda).

L1 / Lasso
Penalty = λ × (sum of |weights|). It pushes many weights to exactly zero, which removes those features. So L1 also does feature selection.
L2 / Ridge
Penalty = λ × (sum of weights²). It shrinks all weights towards zero but rarely to zero. Good when features are correlated with each other.
Elastic Net
L1 and L2 together.
Dropout
For neural networks: randomly switch off some neurons during each training step, so the network can't rely on any single one.
Early stopping
Stop training when the validation error starts rising, even if training error is still falling.

Memory hook: L1 → zeros (sparse). L2 → small. Bigger λ → simpler model.

topics.title: Classic models
topics.html:
Linear regression: predicting a number

Fit a straight line (or a flat plane, with many features) through the data:

prediction = w₁·x₁ + w₂·x₂ + … + b

Each weight w says how much the prediction moves when that feature goes up by 1. Training picks the weights that minimise the MSE (mean squared error): the average of (actual − predicted)². Squaring makes all errors positive and punishes big misses more.

R²
How much of the variation in the target the model explains. 1 = perfect, 0 = no better than always predicting the average. Adding any feature, even a useless one, never lowers R², so adjusted R² adds a penalty for extra features.
Multicollinearity
Two features that move together (height in cm and in inches). Predictions are fine, but the individual weights become unstable and hard to interpret.

Logistic regression: predicting a probability

Despite the name, it is a classification model. It computes the same weighted sum as linear regression, then squashes it through the sigmoid function so the output lands between 0 and 1. That output is read as a probability.

sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z))     z = 0 → 0.5,  big positive z → near 1,  big negative z → near 0

If the probability is above a threshold (usually 0.5), predict "yes". Because the threshold falls where z = 0, and z is a straight-line formula, the decision boundary is a straight line.

It is trained with log loss, also called binary cross-entropy. Log loss punishes a confident wrong answer very hard: predicting 0.99 for something that turned out to be 0 costs far more than predicting 0.6. MSE is not used here because, combined with the sigmoid, it gives a bumpy loss that is hard to minimise.

Why CTR matters

The probability that a user clicks an ad is called CTR (click-through rate). Logistic regression is the classic CTR model because it is fast, works on millions of sparse features, and outputs a probability you can directly use to decide how much to bid.

Softmax is the multi-class version: it turns K scores into K probabilities that add up to 1.

k-nearest neighbours (kNN)

To classify a new point, look at the k closest training points and take a majority vote (or the average, for regression). There's no training step at all; it just stores the data. That is why it's called a lazy learner. All the work happens at prediction time, which is slow on large data.

  • Small k (like 1) follows every noisy point → overfits. Large k smooths too much → underfits.
  • It measures distance, so features must be scaled. Otherwise salary in rupees (0–10,00,000) drowns out age (0–100).
  • With many features, all points end up roughly equally far apart, so "nearest" stops meaning much. This is the curse of dimensionality.

Naive Bayes

Uses Bayes' theorem (see the Stats section) to compute P(class | features). The "naive" part is the assumption that every feature is independent of the others once you know the class. That's rarely true, but the model still works well, especially for text like spam filtering, and it's very fast.

Zero-frequency problem: if a word never appeared with "spam" in training, its probability is 0, and multiplying by 0 wipes out everything. Laplace smoothing fixes it by adding 1 to every count.

Support vector machine (SVM)

Draws the boundary between two classes that leaves the widest possible gap (the margin) to the nearest points of each class. Those nearest points are the support vectors; they alone decide where the boundary goes, and moving any other point changes nothing.

C
How much the SVM hates misclassifying training points. Large C → tries hard to get every point right, narrow margin, risk of overfitting. Small C → wider margin, tolerates some mistakes.
Kernel trick
When the classes can't be split by a straight line, a kernel (like RBF, the radial basis function) lets the SVM act as if the data were mapped into a higher-dimensional space where a straight split works, without computing that mapping.

Two ways to group models

Generative
Learns how each class's data looks, P(features and class). Example: Naive Bayes.
Discriminative
Learns only the boundary, P(class | features). Examples: logistic regression, SVM, decision trees, neural networks.
Parametric
A fixed number of parameters no matter how much data you have. Example: logistic regression.
Non-parametric
Grows with the data. Examples: kNN (stores all points), decision trees.

topics.title: Decision trees & ensembles
topics.html:
Decision trees

A tree asks a series of yes/no questions ("age < 30?", "uses Android?") and each leaf gives a prediction. At every step it picks the question that best separates the classes, measured by how pure (all one class) the resulting groups are.

Gini impurity
1 − Σ pᵢ², where pᵢ is the share of class i in the node. A pure node scores 0. A 50/50 split scores 0.5, the worst for two classes.
Entropy
−Σ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ. Also 0 for a pure node, and 1 for a 50/50 split.
Information gain
Entropy before the split − weighted entropy after it. The tree picks the split with the highest gain.

Worked example

A node has 8 "click" and 2 "no click". p = 0.8 and 0.2. Gini = 1 − (0.64 + 0.04) = 0.32.

  • Trees compare one feature to a threshold at a time, so they don't need feature scaling.
  • A tree allowed to grow fully will memorise the data, so it overfits easily. Limit its depth or prune it.

Ensembles: bagging vs boosting

An ensemble combines many models into one, usually many trees. There are two main styles.

Bagging (short for bootstrap aggregating) trains many trees independently, side by side. Each one sees a different random sample of the rows, drawn with replacement (a bootstrap sample; it contains about 63% of the unique rows). Their predictions are averaged or voted. Each deep tree is noisy, but their mistakes point in different directions and cancel out. So bagging reduces variance.

Random Forest is bagging plus one extra trick: each split may only look at a random subset of the features. That makes the trees more different from each other, so averaging helps even more.

Boosting trains small, weak trees one after another. Each new tree focuses on what the previous ones got wrong: AdaBoost gives the misclassified rows more weight, and gradient boosting fits the next tree to the remaining errors (the residuals). Many weak learners add up to a strong one, so boosting mainly reduces bias. XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are popular, fast versions.

BaggingBoosting
Training orderparallel, independentsequential, each fixes the last
Base treesdeep (overfit-prone)shallow (weak)
Mainly reducesvariancebias
Noisy data / outliersrobustsensitive
ExamplesRandom ForestAdaBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM

A free extra from bagging: each tree never saw about 37% of the rows. Testing each tree on its unseen rows gives a free accuracy estimate, the OOB (out-of-bag) error.

topics.title: Clustering & dimensionality reduction
topics.html:
k-means clustering

Splits the data into k groups. The algorithm:

  1. Place k centre points (centroids) at random.
  2. Assign every point to its nearest centroid.
  3. Move each centroid to the average of the points assigned to it.
  4. Repeat steps 2–3 until nothing changes.
  • You must choose k yourself. The elbow method plots the error against k and picks the bend where adding clusters stops helping much. The silhouette score (−1 to 1, higher is better) measures how well each point fits its cluster.
  • A bad random start can give a bad result. k-means++ picks smarter starting points.
  • It uses averages and distances, so it is sensitive to outliers and needs scaled features. It assumes roughly round, similar-sized clusters.

Other clustering methods

Hierarchical
Start with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merge the two closest. The result is a tree diagram (dendrogram); cut it at any height to get your clusters. No need to pick k up front.
DBSCAN
Density-based. Clusters are areas where points are packed closely together. It finds any shape, doesn't need k, and labels isolated points as noise / outliers.
GMM
Gaussian mixture model. Soft clustering: each point gets a probability of belonging to each cluster. Fitted with the EM (expectation–maximisation) algorithm.

PCA (principal component analysis)

You have 100 columns, many of them overlapping. PCA builds a few new columns, called principal components, that keep most of the information. The first component points in the direction where the data spreads out the most; the second is the next-most-spread direction at a right angle to the first, and so on. Keep the first few, drop the rest.

  • It is unsupervised: it ignores labels.
  • Scale the features first. Otherwise a column measured in big units looks like it has the most spread.
  • Mathematically, the components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and each one's eigenvalue is how much spread it captures.

Worked example

Eigenvalues are 4, 3, 2 and 1 (total 10). The first two components keep (4 + 3)/10 = 70% of the variance.

Don't confuse it with LDA (linear discriminant analysis), which does use labels and looks for directions that separate the classes. t-SNE and UMAP are used mainly to draw high-dimensional data in 2D.

topics.title: Measuring a model
topics.html:
The confusion matrix

For a yes/no classifier, every prediction falls into one of four boxes. The first word says whether the model was right; the second says what it predicted.

Predicted yesPredicted no
Actually yesTP (true positive)FN (false negative), a miss
Actually noFP (false positive), a false alarmTN (true negative)
Accuracy
(TP + TN) / everything. The share of all predictions that were right.
Precision
TP / (TP + FP). Of everything I flagged as yes, how much really was yes? Matters when false alarms are costly: a spam filter must not bin real email.
Recall
TP / (TP + FN). Also called sensitivity or TPR (true positive rate). Of all the real yeses, how many did I catch? Matters when misses are costly: cancer screening, fraud.
F1 score
2 × P × R / (P + R), the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It's only high when both are high.
Specificity
TN / (TN + FP). Recall for the "no" class.

Worked example

TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 30 (100 rows).
Accuracy = 70/100 = 0.70. Precision = 40/50 = 0.80. Recall = 40/60 = 0.67. F1 = 2 × 0.8 × 0.67 / 1.47 ≈ 0.73.

The threshold trade-off. Raise the threshold (say "yes" only when very sure) and precision goes up while recall goes down. Lower it and the opposite happens.

Why accuracy lies on imbalanced data

Only about 1 in 100 ad views gets a click. A model that always says "no click" is 99% accurate and completely useless. When one class is rare, look at precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC or log loss instead.

ROC curve
Plots recall (TPR) against FPR (false positive rate) = FP / (FP + TN), for every possible threshold.
ROC-AUC
The area under that curve. Meaning: pick one random positive and one random negative; AUC is the chance the model scores the positive higher. 0.5 = random guessing, 1 = perfect.
PR-AUC
Area under the precision–recall curve. More honest than ROC-AUC when positives are very rare.
Log loss
Measures how good the predicted probabilities are, not just the yes/no calls. Key in ad-tech, where the probability itself sets the bid.

Regression metrics

MAE
Mean absolute error: average of |actual − predicted|. Easy to read, and robust to outliers.
MSE
Mean squared error. Squaring makes big errors count much more, so it is sensitive to outliers.
RMSE
√MSE, back in the original units.

topics.title: Preparing data & validating fairly
topics.html:
Cross-validation

One train/test split can be lucky or unlucky. k-fold cross-validation splits the data into k parts, trains on k − 1 of them and tests on the remaining one, repeats k times so each part is the test once, and averages the k scores.

Stratified
Each fold keeps the same class proportions as the full data. Use it for imbalanced data.
Time series
Never shuffle. Always train on the past and test on the future, or the model "sees" the future.
Leave-one-out
k = number of rows. Very thorough, very slow.

Data leakage

Leakage means information from the test data, or from the future, sneaks into training. The test score looks great and the real-world score is poor. Common causes:

  • Scaling or filling missing values using the whole dataset before splitting. Always fit these steps on the training data only, then apply them to the test data.
  • A feature that is only known after the outcome, like using "refund issued" to predict "will the customer complain".
  • Shuffling time-ordered data.

Feature preparation

Scaling
Put features on similar ranges. Standardisation makes each one mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Normalisation squeezes into 0–1. Needed for anything based on distances or gradients: kNN, SVM, k-means, PCA, neural networks, regularised regression. Not needed for trees.
One-hot encoding
Turns a category ("red/green/blue") into one 0/1 column per value. Fine for a few values.
Target encoding
Replaces each category with the average label for that category. Works for many values but can leak, so compute it carefully.
Feature hashing
Maps a huge number of categories (millions of app or user IDs) into a fixed number of columns using a hash function. Fixed memory; the cost is that some IDs collide. Standard in ad-tech.
Missing values
Fill with the mean, median or most common value, or add a "was missing" flag column. XGBoost handles missing values on its own.

Imbalanced classes

When one class is rare (fraud, clicks):

  • Give the rare class a bigger weight in the loss (class weights).
  • Oversample the rare class (SMOTE creates synthetic examples between existing ones) or undersample the common one.
  • Move the decision threshold.
  • Judge with precision, recall, F1 or PR-AUC, not accuracy.

Time series in one minute

Data ordered in time, like daily ad impressions. It's made of a trend (long-term up or down), seasonality (repeating patterns, like weekends) and leftover noise. Many classic models need it to be stationary (average and spread don't change over time); differencing (today − yesterday) usually achieves that. ARIMA is the classic model: AR uses past values, I is the differencing, MA uses past errors.

topics.title: Neural networks & transformers
topics.html:
How a neural network learns

A neural network is layers of simple units (neurons). Each neuron takes a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through an activation function, which adds a bend. Without activation functions, any number of layers would collapse into one straight-line model.

Training uses gradient descent: measure the loss, work out which direction each weight should move to reduce it (the gradient), and take a small step that way. Backpropagation is just the chain rule from calculus, used to compute all those gradients efficiently from the output layer backwards.

Learning rate
The size of each step. Too high → the loss jumps around or blows up. Too low → training crawls.
Batch / SGD
Computing the gradient on all data each step is slow. SGD (stochastic gradient descent) uses one row or a small mini-batch per step: noisier but much faster.
Epoch
One full pass over the training data.
Adam
The default optimiser. It adapts the step size for each weight and adds momentum (keeps moving in the recent direction).

Activation functions

Sigmoid
Output 0 to 1. For large inputs it goes flat, so its gradient is almost zero. In deep networks these tiny gradients multiply and shrink to nothing, so early layers stop learning: the vanishing gradient problem.
Tanh
Output −1 to 1. Same flattening issue, a bit better than sigmoid.
ReLU
max(0, x). Cheap, doesn't flatten for positive inputs, the default for hidden layers. A neuron stuck with negative input outputs 0 forever, the dying ReLU problem; Leaky ReLU fixes it with a small slope below 0.
Softmax
For the output layer in multi-class problems: turns scores into probabilities that sum to 1.

Fixes for vanishing gradients: ReLU, residual (skip) connections, batch normalisation, and good starting weights (He initialisation for ReLU, Xavier for tanh/sigmoid). For exploding gradients, cap them with gradient clipping.

CNNs and RNNs

A CNN (convolutional neural network) slides small filters over an image to detect edges, then shapes, then objects. Pooling layers shrink the image and have no weights to learn.

output size = (input − filter + 2 × padding) / stride + 1

Worked example

32×32×3 image, six 5×5 filters, stride 1, no padding. Output = (32 − 5)/1 + 1 = 28, so 28×28×6. Each filter has 5 × 5 × 3 = 75 weights + 1 bias = 76, and 6 filters give 456 parameters.

A fully connected (dense) layer from n inputs to m outputs has n × m + m parameters (weights plus one bias per output).

An RNN (recurrent neural network) reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a memory forward. Plain RNNs forget long-range information because of vanishing gradients. LSTM (long short-term memory) and GRU add gates that decide what to keep and what to forget.

Transformers and LLMs

A transformer processes all the words of a sentence at once instead of one at a time. Its core idea is attention: for each word, it scores how relevant every other word is, then builds a blend of them weighted by those scores. In "the bank of the river", attention lets "bank" look at "river" to pick the right meaning.

  • Each word makes a query (what am I looking for?), a key (what do I contain?) and a value (what I pass on). Relevance = query · key. The scores are divided by √(key size) so they don't get so large that softmax becomes all-or-nothing.
  • Every word looks at every other word, so cost grows with the square of the sequence length.
  • Attention by itself ignores word order, so a positional encoding is added to each word.
BERT
Encoder-only. Trained by hiding random words and guessing them (masked language modelling). Good for understanding tasks like classification.
GPT
Decoder-only. Trained to predict the next word. Good for generating text. LLMs (large language models) like GPT work this way.
Temperature
Controls randomness when generating. Near 0 → always the most likely word (greedy). Higher → more varied.
Fine-tuning
Further training a pre-trained model on your own data. LoRA trains a small add-on instead of all the weights.
RAG
Retrieval-augmented generation: look up relevant documents first and give them to the LLM along with the question.
Embedding
A list of numbers that represents a word, user or ad, where similar things get similar lists. Similarity is often measured by cosine similarity (1 = same direction, 0 = unrelated).

topics.title: Probability & statistics
topics.html:
Bayes' theorem

P(A | B) = P(B | A) · P(A) / P(B)

It flips a conditional: from "how likely is the evidence if A is true" to "how likely is A now that I've seen the evidence". P(B) is the total chance of the evidence, added up over every way it can happen.

Worked example: the classic rare-disease trap

1% of people have a disease. The test catches 99% of sick people, but also flags 5% of healthy people. You test positive. Chance you're sick?

Out of 10,000 people: 100 are sick and 99 of them test positive. 9,900 are healthy and 5% of them, 495, also test positive. So P(sick | positive) = 99 / (99 + 495) ≈ 17%. Because the disease is rare, most positives are false alarms.

Distributions to know

NameDescribesMeanVariance
Bernoulli(p)one yes/no trial, like one ad viewpp(1 − p)
Binomial(n, p)number of yeses in n trialsnpnp(1 − p)
Poisson(λ)count of events in a time windowλλ
Geometric(p)trials until the first yes1/p(1 − p)/p²
Uniform(a, b)every value equally likely(a + b)/2(b − a)²/12
Normal(μ, σ²)the bell curveμσ²

Normal rule of thumb: about 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2, and 99.7% within 3.

Two rules for variance: Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X), since adding a constant doesn't change spread. Covariance = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y].

Sampling and the central limit theorem

The CLT (central limit theorem): take many samples of size n and compute each sample's average. Those averages form a normal (bell) curve, whatever shape the original data had. Its spread, the standard error, is σ/√n. So to halve the standard error you need 4× the data.

Hypothesis testing and A/B tests

You show half the users ad A and half ad B. B gets a higher CTR. Is it really better, or just luck?

H₀
The null hypothesis: "no real difference".
p-value
If H₀ were true, the chance of seeing a difference at least this big by luck. Small p-value (below α, usually 0.05) → reject H₀. It is not the probability that H₀ is true.
Type I error
A false positive: concluding B is better when it isn't. Its probability is α.
Type II error
A false negative: missing a real improvement. Its probability is β.
Power
1 − β, the chance of catching a real effect. More data → more power.

Comparing two click rates uses a two-proportion z-test (or a chi-square test). Classic mistakes: checking results every day and stopping as soon as it looks significant (peeking), and testing many things at once without correcting for it.

Simpson's paradox: a trend that holds in every group can reverse when the groups are combined. Correlation is not causation, and zero correlation does not mean independence.

Quick expected-value facts

  • Expected rolls of a fair die until a 6: 6 (1/p for p = 1/6).
  • Expected coin tosses until the first head: 2. Until two heads in a row: 6.
  • Two coins, at least one is heads. P(both heads) = 1/3 (HH, HT, TH are equally likely).
  • MLE (maximum likelihood estimation) picks the parameters that make the observed data most likely. Adding a prior belief gives MAP; a normal prior on the weights is the same as L2 regularisation.

topics.title: Applied ML: ads, recommendations & drift
topics.html:
How an ad gets picked

When you open an app, an auction runs in about 100 milliseconds (RTB, real-time bidding). For each candidate ad, models predict the chance you'll click (pCTR) and the chance you'll then install or buy (pCVR, conversion rate). The bid is roughly value × pCTR × pCVR. Ads are ranked by eCPM (effective cost per thousand impressions) = CTR × cost per click × 1000.

  • Because the predicted probability is plugged straight into the bid, it must be calibrated: if the model says 2%, about 2% should actually click. Accuracy and AUC can't tell you this; log loss can.
  • Training sets often keep only some of the "no click" rows to save time (negative downsampling). That makes predictions too high, so they must be corrected afterwards.
  • Typical CTR models: logistic regression on hashed features, factorization machines (learn how pairs of features interact), gradient-boosted trees, and deep models like Wide & Deep.

Recommendations, exploration and drift

Collaborative filtering
"Users like you also liked…". Matrix factorization splits the big user × item table into a small user table and a small item table of hidden tastes.
Cold start
A new user or ad has no history. Fall back on its content features or overall popularity.
Bandits
Should you keep showing the ad that works best now (exploit) or try new ones that might be better (explore)? Multi-armed bandit methods balance this: ε-greedy, UCB (upper confidence bound), Thompson sampling.
NDCG
A ranking metric that rewards putting good items near the top of the list.
Drift
User behaviour changes over time, so a model quietly gets worse. Monitor it and retrain regularly.
Isolation Forest
An anomaly detector, used for click fraud. Odd points get separated from the rest in very few random splits.
Attribution
Deciding which ad gets credit for an install: last click, first click, or split across all touches.

Common traps to remember

  • Bagging → less variance. Boosting → less bias.
  • L1 → weights become zero. L2 → weights become small.
  • Trees don't need scaling; kNN, SVM, k-means, PCA and neural nets do.
  • Logistic regression is for classification.
  • 99% accuracy on 99%-negative data means nothing.
  • A p-value is not the chance that H₀ is true.
  • Never shuffle time-series data.

quiz.q: Training accuracy is 99% but test accuracy is 70%. What's happening?
options: The learning rate is too low
quiz.why: The model does great on data it has seen and much worse on new data, so it memorised noise instead of learning the general pattern. That's overfitting.

quiz.q: Both training and test error are high. Best first fix?
options: Use a more complex model or more features
Collect more of the same data
quiz.why: High error everywhere means the model is too simple to capture the pattern (underfitting). Regularisation and dropout would make it even simpler.

quiz.q: Which regularisation can make some weights exactly zero?
quiz.why: L1's penalty pushes weights all the way to zero, which effectively deletes those features. L2 only makes weights small.

quiz.q: Increasing the regularisation strength λ will usually:
quiz.why: A bigger penalty forces a simpler model: it's less able to fit noise (lower variance) but also less able to fit the real pattern (higher bias).

quiz.q: Predicting tomorrow's number of ad clicks is a:
quiz.why: The answer is a number, not a category, so it's regression. 'Will this user click: yes/no?' would be classification.

quiz.q: Grouping users into segments without any labels is:
quiz.why: There's no 'right answer' column to learn from, so the model has to find structure by itself. That's unsupervised learning, specifically clustering.

quiz.q: Logistic regression is mainly used for:
quiz.why: Despite the name, it outputs a probability between 0 and 1 and then applies a threshold to pick a class.

quiz.q: Logistic regression is trained by minimising:
quiz.why: Log loss heavily punishes confident wrong probabilities. MSE combined with the sigmoid gives a bumpy loss that's hard to minimise; hinge loss is for SVMs and Gini is for trees.

quiz.q: The decision boundary of plain logistic regression is:
options: A step function of each feature
quiz.why: It predicts 'yes' when the weighted sum is above 0, and 'weighted sum = 0' is a straight line (or flat plane).

quiz.q: Which algorithm is a 'lazy learner' with no real training phase?
quiz.why: kNN just stores the training data. All the work (finding the nearest neighbours) happens when you ask it to predict.

quiz.q: In kNN, using k = 1 tends to:
quiz.why: With k = 1 each prediction copies a single neighbour, so every noisy point affects the result. Larger k smooths things out.

quiz.q: Which of these is a generative model?
quiz.why: Naive Bayes models how the data of each class looks (P(features and class)). The others only learn the boundary between classes.

quiz.q: What is the 'naive' assumption in Naive Bayes?
options: Features are independent given the class
quiz.why: It assumes that once you know the class, knowing one feature tells you nothing about another. Rarely true, but it works well in practice.

quiz.q: In an SVM, which training points decide where the boundary goes?
options: The points furthest from the boundary
quiz.why: Only the points closest to the boundary (the support vectors) matter. You could delete every other point and get the same boundary.

quiz.q: A very large C in an SVM leads to:
options: A wider margin and more errors allowed
A narrower margin and a risk of overfitting
quiz.why: C is the penalty for misclassifying training points. Large C means the SVM bends over backwards to get every point right, shrinking the margin.

quiz.q: Adding a completely useless feature to linear regression makes R²:
options: Stay the same or go up
quiz.why: R² can never fall when you add a feature, which is why adjusted R² exists: it penalises extra features.

quiz.q: Which algorithm does NOT need feature scaling?
quiz.why: A tree compares one feature to a threshold at a time ('age < 30?'), so the units don't matter. The others all use distances or gradients.

quiz.q: Gini impurity of a node with a 50/50 split of two classes:
quiz.why: Gini = 1 − (0.5² + 0.5²) = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5, the worst possible value for two classes. A pure node would be 0.

quiz.q: Entropy of a pure node (all one class):
quiz.why: There's no uncertainty at all about the class, so entropy is 0. A 50/50 node would have entropy 1.

quiz.q: A node has 8 'click' and 2 'no click'. Gini impurity?
Bagging mainly reduces:
quiz.why: It averages many independently trained deep trees. Their individual noise points in different directions and cancels out, so variance drops.

quiz.q: Boosting mainly reduces:
quiz.why: Each new weak tree fixes the remaining errors of the ensemble, so together they fit patterns a single weak tree couldn't. That lowers bias.

quiz.q: What does Random Forest add on top of plain bagging?
options: A random subset of features at each split
quiz.why: Restricting each split to random features makes the trees more different from each other, so averaging cancels more noise. Sequential training and reweighting are boosting ideas.

quiz.q: Which ensemble can be trained fully in parallel?
quiz.why: Random Forest's trees don't depend on each other. Boosting trees must be built one after another, because each needs the previous ones' errors.

quiz.q: Roughly what fraction of unique rows ends up in one bootstrap sample?
quiz.why: Sampling n rows with replacement includes about 1 − 1/e ≈ 63% of the unique rows. The other ~37% are 'out-of-bag' and give a free error estimate.

quiz.q: Which ensemble is more hurt by noisy labels and outliers?
quiz.why: Boosting keeps focusing on the examples it gets wrong, and mislabelled points are always wrong, so it ends up chasing noise.

quiz.q: The elbow method helps you choose:
quiz.why: Plot the clustering error against k and pick the point where adding more clusters stops helping much (the 'elbow').

quiz.q: Which clustering method doesn't need k and labels outliers as noise?
quiz.why: DBSCAN grows clusters through dense regions and leaves isolated points unassigned as noise. It also finds clusters of any shape.

quiz.q: Which is most sensitive to outliers?
quiz.why: k-means moves each centre to the average of its points, and a single far-away point drags an average a long way.

quiz.q: PCA is:
options: Unsupervised; finds directions of maximum spread
quiz.why: It ignores labels and builds new axes along which the data spreads out the most, then keeps the top few.

quiz.q: PCA eigenvalues are 4, 3, 2, 1. Variance kept by the first two components?
quiz.why: Each eigenvalue is the spread captured by its component. (4 + 3) / (4 + 3 + 2 + 1) = 7/10 = 70%.

quiz.q: Why scale features before PCA?
options: Otherwise features in large units dominate the components
quiz.why: PCA looks for the largest spread. Salary in rupees has a far bigger numeric spread than age in years, so it would take over without scaling.

quiz.q: The silhouette score ranges from:
quiz.why: Near 1 = the point sits well inside its own cluster; near 0 = on a border; negative = probably in the wrong cluster.

quiz.q: 99% of rows are negative and the model always predicts negative. Accuracy?
quiz.why: It gets every negative right, which is 99% of rows, while catching zero positives. This is why accuracy is useless on imbalanced data.

quiz.q: TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 30. Precision?
quiz.why: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 40 / 50 = 0.80. Of everything flagged positive, 80% really was.

quiz.q: Same matrix (TP 40, FP 10, FN 20, TN 30). Recall?
quiz.why: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 40 / 60 ≈ 0.67. Of all real positives, the model caught two-thirds.

quiz.q: For cancer screening, the most important metric is usually:
quiz.why: Missing a sick patient (a false negative) is far worse than a false alarm, so you want to catch as many real cases as possible: recall.

quiz.q: For a spam filter where losing a real email is very bad, focus on:
quiz.why: Here the costly mistake is a false positive (a real email marked spam). Precision measures how trustworthy the 'spam' label is.

quiz.q: The ROC curve plots:
quiz.why: For every threshold, the ROC curve plots the true positive rate (recall) against the false positive rate.

quiz.q: An AUC of 0.5 means:
quiz.why: AUC is the chance the model ranks a random positive above a random negative. 0.5 is a coin flip.

quiz.q: Raising the classification threshold usually:
quiz.why: You say 'yes' only when very sure, so fewer false alarms (precision up) but more real positives slip through (recall down).

quiz.q: Why is F1 the harmonic mean instead of the simple average?
options: It stays low unless both precision and recall are high
quiz.why: With precision 1.0 and recall 0.0, the simple average is 0.5 but F1 is 0. The harmonic mean punishes one of them being bad.

quiz.q: Which regression metric is most robust to outliers?
quiz.why: MAE uses the plain absolute error. MSE and RMSE square errors, so one huge miss dominates them.

quiz.q: For CTR prediction (about 1% positives), which pair of metrics is most useful?
quiz.why: PR-AUC handles heavy imbalance well, and log loss checks the quality of the probabilities themselves, which matter because they set the bid.

quiz.q: Which of these is data leakage?
options: Fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting
quiz.why: The scaler's average and spread then include test rows, so test information sneaks into training. Fit on the training split only.

quiz.q: Best way to validate a time-series model?
options: Train on the past, test on the future
quiz.why: Shuffling would let the model train on the future and test on the past, which can never happen in real life.

quiz.q: Stratified k-fold keeps:
options: The same number of features in each fold
The same class proportions in each fold
quiz.why: Each fold gets roughly the same mix of classes as the full data, which matters when one class is rare.

quiz.q: Leave-one-out CV on 1,000 rows trains how many models?
quiz.why: Each row is the test set once, so you train 1,000 models, each on the other 999 rows.

quiz.q: Best way to encode millions of distinct app IDs with limited memory?
quiz.why: Hashing maps any number of IDs into a fixed number of columns. One-hot would create millions of columns.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a way to handle class imbalance?
options: Judging the model only by accuracy
quiz.why: Accuracy hides the problem (see the 99% example). The other three are all standard fixes.

quiz.q: Which activation is most associated with vanishing gradients?
quiz.why: Sigmoid goes flat for large inputs, so its gradient is tiny (at most 0.25). Many tiny numbers multiplied through layers shrink to almost zero.

quiz.q: Training loss jumps around wildly and then blows up. Likely cause?
quiz.why: Each step is so big that it overshoots the minimum and lands higher each time. Lower the learning rate.

quiz.q: A deep network with no activation functions is equivalent to:
quiz.why: Stacking linear layers just gives another linear function. Activation functions are what let the network learn curves.

quiz.q: 32×32×3 input, six 5×5 filters, stride 1, no padding. Output size?
quiz.why: (32 − 5 + 0)/1 + 1 = 28, and there's one output channel per filter: 28×28×6.

quiz.q: A dense layer from 100 inputs to 50 outputs has how many parameters?
quiz.why: 100 × 50 weights + 50 biases (one per output) = 5,050.

quiz.q: How many parameters does a max-pooling layer have?
quiz.why: Pooling just takes the maximum in each window. There's nothing to learn.

quiz.q: Output layer and loss for picking one of 10 classes?
quiz.why: Softmax turns 10 scores into probabilities that sum to 1, and cross-entropy rewards giving high probability to the correct class.

quiz.q: Dropout is applied:
quiz.why: Neurons are switched off randomly while training so the network doesn't rely on any one of them. At test time all neurons are used.

quiz.q: Why do transformers divide attention scores by √(key size)?
options: To stop scores getting so large that softmax becomes all-or-nothing
quiz.why: Large dot products push softmax towards one 1 and all 0s, where gradients vanish. Scaling keeps the scores moderate.

quiz.q: Why do transformers need positional encodings?
options: Attention alone has no sense of word order
quiz.why: Attention compares every word with every other word without caring about position, so 'dog bites man' would look like 'man bites dog' without them.

quiz.q: GPT-style models are trained to:
quiz.why: GPT is decoder-only and predicts the next token from the ones before. Filling in hidden words is how BERT is trained.

quiz.q: Setting the sampling temperature close to 0 makes an LLM:
options: Almost always pick the most likely word
quiz.why: Low temperature sharpens the probabilities so the top word nearly always wins. That's close to greedy decoding.

quiz.q: 1% have a disease. The test catches 99% of sick people and flags 5% of healthy ones. P(sick | positive)?
quiz.why: Per 10,000 people: 99 true positives and 495 false positives. 99 / 594 ≈ 17%. When the disease is rare, most positives are false alarms.

quiz.q: Mean and variance of a Poisson distribution with rate λ?
quiz.why: For a Poisson distribution the mean and the variance are both λ. (1/λ and 1/λ² belong to the exponential distribution.)

quiz.q: An ad with CTR 0.3 is shown 10 times. Mean and variance of clicks?
quiz.why: Binomial: mean = np = 3, variance = np(1 − p) = 3 × 0.7 = 2.1.

quiz.q: A p-value of 0.03 with α = 0.05 means:
quiz.why: 0.03 is below the 0.05 cut-off, so the result would be unlikely if there were no real difference. It does NOT mean H₀ has a 3% chance of being true.

quiz.q: A Type I error is:
quiz.why: Rejecting H₀ when it's actually true: you declare a winner that isn't really better.

quiz.q: To halve the standard error of a sample mean, you need:
quiz.why: Standard error = σ/√n. Halving it means doubling √n, which means 4× n.

quiz.q: Var(2X + 3) equals:
quiz.why: Adding a constant doesn't change spread, and multiplying by 2 multiplies variance by 2² = 4.

quiz.q: Expected number of rolls of a fair die to get the first 6?
quiz.why: Waiting for a success with probability p takes 1/p tries on average. 1 / (1/6) = 6.

quiz.q: Two fair coins are tossed and at least one is heads. P(both heads)?
quiz.why: The possible outcomes are HH, HT and TH, all equally likely. Only one of the three is HH.

quiz.q: Best test to compare the click rates of two ad creatives?
quiz.why: Each creative has a share of clicks (a proportion), and this test checks whether two proportions really differ.

quiz.q: Zero correlation between X and Y means:
options: There is no linear relationship, but they may still be related
quiz.why: Y = X² over a symmetric range has zero correlation but depends completely on X. Correlation only measures straight-line relationships.

quiz.q: The classic baseline model for CTR prediction is:
quiz.why: It outputs a probability, trains fast on huge sparse data, and is easy to calibrate. It's been the industry baseline for years.

quiz.q: Why must CTR predictions be well calibrated?
options: The predicted probability directly sets the bid
quiz.why: If the model says 4% when the true rate is 2%, the system bids double what the ad is worth.

quiz.q: You keep only 10% of 'no click' rows when training. The predicted CTRs will be:
options: Too high, so they must be corrected
quiz.why: Clicks now make up a much bigger share of the training data than in reality, so the model overestimates. You rescale the outputs afterwards.

quiz.q: A new ad with no history is an example of:
quiz.why: Collaborative methods need past interactions. Without any, you rely on the ad's content features, popularity, or exploration.

quiz.q: Thompson sampling and UCB address:
quiz.why: They're multi-armed bandit methods: they decide when to keep showing the best-known ad and when to try others that might be better.

quiz.q: A model works well at launch and gets worse over the following weeks. Most likely:
quiz.why: User behaviour and the ad mix change over time, so the patterns the model learned slowly go stale. Monitor and retrain.

quiz.q: Isolation Forest is used for:
quiz.why: It splits the data randomly. Unusual points get isolated in very few splits, which flags them as anomalies.
